title: Why 9/11 Baffles Us 25 Years Later
gist: Reviewing Peter Bergen's All the Presidents' Wars, Michael Hirsh argues the war on terror was a self-inflicted strategic disaster that mistook a ~1,000-person nonstate group for an existential threat, and warns that Trump's February 2026 Iran war repeats the Iraq template — draining U.S. firepower, adding debt, weakening Washington's regional position and potentially reigniting al Qaeda.

themes.theme: The 2026 Iran war as Iraq redux

insights.claim: Trump's February 2026 war with Iran has weakened the U.S. role in the Middle East, seriously drained U.S. military firepower and piled on more debt, while possibly giving Tehran new advantages in the near term.
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: Munitions and missile-defense restocking plus a wider deficit are the direct fiscal consequences; watch supplemental defense appropriations and Treasury supply as the transmission channel.
insights.quote: the war has further weakened the U.S. role in the region while, once again, seriously draining its military firepower and piling on ever more debt
insights.locator: Now, in 2026, President Donald Trump’s latest war

insights.claim: The prolonged U.S.-Iran conflict may be reigniting the fading embers of al Qaeda, reintroducing jihadist-attack risk that had been largely dormant.
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: A renewed terror-attack tail risk argues for keeping some optionality in defense/security names and in geopolitical hedges that had been faded since the 2010s.
insights.quote: The prolonged conflict may also be reigniting the fading embers of al Qaeda.
insights.locator: Now, in 2026, President Donald Trump’s latest war

insights.claim: Bergen judges that Trump's justification for the Iran war was as flimsy as Bush's for Iraq because there was no evidence the Iranian regime posed any pressing threat to the United States.
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: A war launched on weak public justification is more vulnerable to domestic political reversal — a source of policy-path volatility for oil and regional risk assets.
insights.quote: there was no evidence that the Iranian regime posed any pressing threat to the United States
insights.locator: As for Trump, his justification for launching a new war

insights.claim: A U.S. Army study concluded that the only victor to emerge from the 2003 Iraq war was an emboldened and expansionist Iran — the same regime Washington is now fighting again.
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: Historical base rate: U.S. military intervention in the region has repeatedly strengthened the adversary it targeted — a reason to discount clean 'regime collapse' scenarios in Iran pricing.
insights.quote: the only victor” to come out of the 2003 Iraq war appeared to be “an emboldened and expansionist Iran
insights.locator: The Middle East quagmire only seems to grow deeper

themes.theme: Opportunity cost: the Great Distraction and China

insights.claim: While Washington repurposed its military for counterinsurgency and precision counterterrorism, Beijing built a force designed to fight and defeat a peer competitor — and the U.S. is still trying to catch up.
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: The peer-competition capability gap is the structural driver of U.S. shipbuilding, long-range fires and munitions procurement — a multi-year budget priority independent of who is president.
insights.quote: while Washington was repurposing the U.S. military to engage in massive counterinsurgency campaigns and precision counterterrorism operations, Beijing was busy building a military to fight and defeat a peer-level competitor
insights.locator: How did a tiny, ragtag group of jihadists

insights.claim: The post-9/11 global war on terror is by far the longest war in U.S. history, and one U.S. general labeled the period the 'era of the Great Distraction.'
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: Frames the 25-year misallocation of U.S. defense capital as the origin of today's catch-up spending cycle in peer-conflict capabilities.
insights.quote: the “era of the Great Distraction” following 9/11
insights.locator: How did a tiny, ragtag group of jihadists

insights.claim: The war on terror cost trillions of dollars plus hundreds of thousands of American and Iraqi lives and limbs — a scale of expenditure reserved for existential threats, applied to what Gen. Anthony Zinni calls a band of maybe a thousand radicals.
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: A canonical case study in threat mispricing — useful as a prior when markets extrapolate small shocks into structural regimes.
insights.quote: This was not an existential threat,” Zinni said. “It was a band of maybe a thousand radicals.
insights.locator: That is why Marine Gen. Anthony Zinni

themes.theme: Threat mispricing as a repeatable framework

insights.claim: Bin Laden's success came from fooling Washington into thinking al Qaeda was far bigger and better-resourced than it actually was — the adversary's main weapon was the overreaction it provoked.
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: A reusable model: an actor's real leverage can be the size of the response it induces, not its own capability — applies to terrorism, cyber and market panics alike.
insights.quote: bin Laden achieved this success by fooling the Americans into thinking he was much more threatening—much bigger and better-resourced—than he really was
insights.locator: If the Iraq war was a titanic mistake

insights.claim: Bin Laden explicitly targeted 'bleeding America to the point of bankruptcy' in a 2004 Al Jazeera video and said he found it easy to provoke and bait the administration — the economic drain was the stated strategy, not a byproduct.
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: Attrition-by-provocation is a cheap asymmetric strategy any adversary can copy; the fiscal cost of responding is the real exposure.
insights.quote: bleeding America to the point of bankruptcy
insights.locator: Yet bin Laden wasn’t a complete fool

insights.claim: Documents from bin Laden's Abbottabad compound show al Qaeda had no post-9/11 plan and was in 'disarray' and 'afflicted' — the group never recovered, implying it was a marginal enemy that could have been eliminated quickly.
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: Evidence that the 25-year security build-out was calibrated to a phantom, which supports skepticism of open-ended threat narratives used to justify spending.
insights.quote: bin Laden’s “post-9/11 goals did not go beyond empty threats, unexecuted plans, and more than a little wishful thinking.
insights.locator: Al Qaeda, in other words, had only one A-team

insights.claim: Conflating distinct actors — the Taliban with al Qaeda, Saddam with terrorism — was the specific analytical error that turned a narrow special-ops mission into an endless global war; Bush is dubbed the 'Great Conflater.'
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: Category error in threat definition is the mechanism that converts a bounded problem into an unbounded liability — check for the same conflation in current Iran and China framing.
insights.quote: history should remember George W. Bush as the Great Conflater
insights.locator: That last mistake was, in some ways, the most consequential

insights.claim: The Iraq debacle is argued to have discredited the traditional Republican agenda enough to open the path for Trump's takeover of the party, making the war a root cause of today's U.S. political realignment.
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: Links foreign-policy failure to durable domestic policy volatility — the tariff-and-disruption regime has deep roots and is unlikely to be reversed by one election.
insights.quote: Conservatism was never the same after the first improvised explosive device detonated in Baghdad
insights.locator: Some analysts have argued that the botched response

insights.claim: The Iraq invasion expanded rather than depleted the jihadist pool — Bush's own 2006 National Intelligence Estimate found the Iraq conflict had become the jihadist cause celebre and was shaping a new generation of terrorist leaders.
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: Intervention can be recruitment-positive for the adversary; apply this to forecasting the durability of any Iran-related instability.
insights.quote: the pool of potential terrorists expanded quite dramatically because of the Iraq War
insights.locator: In his book, Bergen does capture some of this absurdity

insights.claim: Bergen's defense of the record — no large-scale foreign-terrorist attack on U.S. soil in 25 years, and the ISIS caliphate destroyed with only 5,000 U.S. troops versus 150,000 a decade earlier — is conceded as tactical success but dismissed as circular given Washington created most of those jihadists.
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: Success metrics that ignore endogenous threat creation overstate policy effectiveness — a caution for evaluating any current security or sanctions program.
insights.quote: the war against ISIS ended the group’s territorial caliphate” with only a small force of 5,000 U.S. soldiers, compared to 150,000 a decade earlier
insights.locator: Indeed, the post-9/11 period was not even remotely comparable

insights.claim: The strategic diversion to Iraq was never subjected to a single cabinet meeting asking whether it was a good idea, with hubris and a desire to reassert U.S. power the best available explanation.
insights.speaker: Michael Hirsh
insights.so_what: Major state decisions can bypass deliberation entirely — process quality is a weak constraint, so policy tail risk is fatter than institutional models imply.
insights.quote: There’s a feeling we’ve got to do something that counts—and bombing some caves is not something that counts
insights.locator: The reasons for the turn to Iraq remain murky
